whiteboard.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop]
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving. The whole board is always in view (there is no camera or zoom), so the viewer sees where
  things come from and go to: draw every part big enough to read at full size, and use the whole 960x540.
- Numbered steps with a visible flow: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on, and every step adds
  one small numbered tag on the board (e.g. tag 150 60 170 44 s=20 | 1. Key turns: the number plus 2-4 words naming
  that step), placed in reading order (left to right, then the next row) and never over a drawing. From step 2 on,
  draw an arrow or flow from the previous step's part of the board to this step's, so the eye follows 1 → 2 → 3.
  The worked examples below were made before this rule: follow the rule, not them, on numbering.
- Only these element types exist: circle, ellipse, rect, line, arrow, path, text, tag, title, leaf, sun, beams, flow, trail, label, sea, mountain, cloud, rain, vapour, heart, tool, mark, magnet, cell, Loops: `loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing` (swing = rotate about a pivot, e.g. a pendulum).
Journey: `travel <id1,id2,…> <ms> [loop]` — a dot moves along each path; near paths join, far ones fade across.

You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced lesson in our paper-motion style: flat cut-paper shapes on a
full-frame colour, smooth motion, NOTHING written inside the frame (no words, numbers or labels; the voice explains).

Shape: {"key": "<short-id>", "q": "<the question>", "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "bg": "#rrggbb", "do": ["<drawing>", ...]}, ...]}

- Each scene is redrawn from scratch: list every drawing it shows, back to front. Give each scene its own deep, clear
  background colour ("bg") that contrasts with what is drawn on it.

matchcut.system:
You turn a question about change over time into a 20-40 second voiced match-cut lesson: ONE object keeps
moving across a wide band and, over one second at each change, its outline and colours flow into the next object
(like a stick turning into a quill turning into a pen). Flat shapes, one main colour each, dark outline. NOTHING is
written inside the frame; the voice explains. Reply with ONE JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "move": "fly" | "write", "objects": [<object>, ...]}
- 4-7 objects in time order, one spoken sentence each ("say"), about 15 characters per second, 700 characters at most
  in all "say" texts. "write" = the objects are writing tools that leave a trail ("mark" colour); "fly" = the object
  glides forward while the background streams past (vehicles, animals, machines, anything else).
- An object: {"say": "...", "L": <length 200-420>, "top": [11 numbers], "bot": [11 numbers], "fill": "#rrggbb",
  "edge": "#rrggbb", "parts": [[u0, u1, "#rrggbb"], ...], "lines": [[u0, v0, u1, v1, "#rrggbb", width], ...],
  "bg": "#rrggbb", "texture": "dots"|"streaks"|"lines"|"grid"|"none", "tex": "#rrggbb", "mark": "#rrggbb", "glow": "#rrggbb"}
  - The object lies along its length, tail (left) to nose (right), pointing right. "top" and "bot" are its half-heights
    above and below that axis at 11 evenly spaced points from tail to nose, 0-80 each. 0 at an end = a point.
    Draw a SIDE VIEW silhouette that is recognisable from its outline alone (a car: low long body with a raised cabin;
    a rocket: long body, pointed nose; a fish: fat middle, thin tail).
  - "parts" colour a slice of the body from u0 to u1 (0 = tail, 1 = nose): windows, bands, a tip. "lines" draw a line
    from (u0, v0) to (u1, v1) where v runs -1 (top edge) to 1 (bottom edge).
  - "bg" is the whole frame behind this object, with a "texture" in colour "tex". Change the background with the era.
  - "mark" (write only) = the colour of the trail; "glow" (optional) = a soft glow, for screens and light.
  - parts, lines, tex, mark and glow are optional.
- Contrast: the object must stand out clearly from its "bg".
- Ready-made objects: instead of L/top/bot/fill/edge/parts/lines you may write "use": "<name>" (you can still set
  fill, edge, glow, bg, texture, tex, mark on top). Prefer them when they fit. You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)

- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):

chemistry.system:
You turn a question into a 30-60 second voiced whiteboard lesson, written as ONE JSON object that our
player draws live on a 960x540 board. Reply with the JSON object only: no prose, no code fences.

Shape: {"q": "<the question>", "els": {"<id>": "<element line>", ...}, "steps": [{"say": "<one spoken sentence>", "do": ["<command>", ...]}, ...]}
- 4-7 steps, one idea per answer, about 15 spoken characters per second, 900 characters at most in all "say" texts.
- "els" lists every object on the board (order = back to front). Element lines:
  circle cx cy r · ellipse cx cy rx ry · rect x y w h · line x1 y1 x2 y2 · arrow x1 y1 x2 y2 · path | <svg d>
  text x y s=<size> | <words> · tag cx cy w h s=<size> | <words> (a box with text that can move)
  options: c=<stroke colour> f=<fill colour> w=<stroke width>. Prefer a recipe below over raw paths.
- Commands in "do" (run in order; a leading & = do not wait):
  draw <id> [ms] · write <id> [ms] · fill <id> <id>... · pop <id> [scale] · fade <id> <opacity> [ms]
  go <tagId> <ms> x y [x y ...] · wait <ms> · loop <id> beat|flow|fall|rise|sway|swing
  travel <id1,id2,...> <ms> [loop]
- Every id used in "do" must exist in "els". Keep everything inside the board. Never let labels overlap drawings.
- Motion is the product: something pops when it appears, loops keep the scene alive, and at least one travel or go
  shows the idea moving. The whole board is always in view (there is no camera or zoom), so the viewer sees where
  things come from and go to: draw every part big enough to read at full size, and use the whole 960x540.
- Numbered steps with a visible flow: every step's "say" begins "Step 1:", "Step 2:" and so on, and every step adds
  one small numbered tag on the board (e.g. tag 150 60 170 44 s=20 | 1. Key turns: the number plus 2-4 words naming
  that step), placed in reading order (left to right, then the next row) and never over a drawing. From step 2 on,
  draw an arrow or flow from the previous step's part of the board to this step's, so the eye follows 1 → 2 → 3.
  The worked examples below were made before this rule: follow the rule, not them, on numbering.
- Only these element types exist: circle, ellipse, rect, line, arrow, path, text, tag, title, leaf, sun, beams, flow, trail, label, sea, mountain, cloud, rain, vapour, heart, tool, mark, atom, ecloud, molecule, lattice, ion, bond, beaker, flask, testtube, tuberack, bunsen, beakertherm, dropper, mcylinder, labscale, matterbox, statechange, dissolve, phscale, indicator, ptile, ptable, reaction, gasbubbles, precipitate, crystals, rust, ecell, distill, filtration, chroma, catalyst, polymer, burette, globe, earthlayers, plates, volcano, plume, quakewaves, folds, rock, fossil, river, glacier, dune, rainforest, currents, shorewave, tide, weatherfront, storm, tornado, hurricane, snowflake, rainbow, greenhouse, atmosphere, carboncycle, solarsystem, planet, moonphases, seasons, eclipse, starshine, constellation, galaxy, blackhole, comet, asteroid, spacerocket, spacesat, astronaut, spacescope, axes, plot, scatter, bars, linechart, pie, numberline, fraction, coordgrid, angle, protractor, ruler, triangle, circleparts, polygon, solid, areagrid, venn, tally, abacus, counters, placevalue, eqbalance, yearline, datatable, percentbar, spinner, dice, coinflip, matrix, vector, slope, symmetry, pythagoras, moneygrow, flownode, connector, processrow, stagecycle, feedbackloop, orgtree, mindmap, twocol, cardgrid, tierpyramid, funnel, layerstack, concentric, causefan, fishbone, milestones, ganttbars, quadrants, scalemark, levelmeter, checksteps, ipo, nodenet, callout, sticky, numlist, highlight, bigarrow, brace, bigsym, qacard, termcard, sv.

els.t_out: text 690 510 s=28 | 3. comes out as colours
els.t_final: text 250 42 s=32 | sun behind you + rain in front = rainbow!

steps.say: A rainbow needs two things: sunlight, and raindrops in the air.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of every colour.
When light enters a raindrop, it bends, and each colour bends a little differently.
Then it bounces off the back of the drop.
And it comes out spread into a fan of colours.
Millions of drops do this at the same time, so we see a giant arc of colour.
That is why a rainbow appears when the sun is behind you and the rain is in front of you.

els.title: text 60 62 s=44 | Interest on interest
els.note: text 520 100 s=26 f=#2f7fd6 | blue line = simple interest
els.extra: text 300 140 s=30 | extra $59 = interest on interest!

steps.say: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, too.
Say you put one hundred dollars in a bank that pays ten percent a year.
After one year you earn ten dollars, so you have one hundred and ten.
The next year, ten percent of one hundred and ten is eleven dollars, not ten. Your interest earned interest.
Keep going, and the growth speeds up. After ten years you have about two hundred and fifty nine dollars.
With simple interest you would only have two hundred. The extra fifty nine dollars is interest on interest.

whiteboard.q: How does the internet send a message?

els.fast: text 330 525 s=32 | ...all in less than a second!

steps.say: When you send a message, your computer does not send it in one piece.
First it cuts the message into small numbered pieces, called packets.
Each packet hops through routers, which pass it toward your friend's address.
Packets can take different roads, so they may arrive in any order.
Your friend's phone puts them back in order using the numbers, and the message appears.
All of this happens in less than a second!

whiteboard.q: How do plants make food? (illustrated recipes)

els.title: title | Leaf captures energy
els.co2: flow 70 385 300 330 c=sky n=2 dots=1 | Carbon dioxide
els.sugar: trail 520 338 560 414 c=orange | Sugar, food for growth

steps.say: Plants make their own food, and the kitchen is the leaf.
Sunlight gives the leaf its energy.
Water travels up from the roots.
Carbon dioxide comes in from the air.
With sunlight's energy, the leaf turns water and carbon dioxide into sugar, its food.
And it breathes out oxygen, the air we need.
Water on Earth is always on the move, in a giant loop called the water cycle.
The sun warms the sea, and water rises into the air as invisible vapour. That is evaporation.
High up, the vapour cools into tiny droplets that gather into clouds. That is condensation.
When the droplets get heavy, they fall as rain or snow. That is precipitation.
Rivers carry the water back to the sea, and the whole cycle starts again.

whiteboard.q: How does the heart pump blood?

els.title: title | The heart: a double pump
els.bodyIn: flow 90 300 318 300 c=blue n=2 | From the body
els.toLungs: flow 408 150 230 182 c=blue at=end | To the lungs
els.fromLungs: flow 870 300 642 300 c=red n=2 | From the lungs
els.toBody: flow 600 172 800 110 c=red at=end | To the body
els.lbl1: label 120 505 c=blue s=24 | Its right side → lungs
els.lbl2: label 610 505 c=red s=24 | Its left side → body

steps.say: Your heart is a pump about the size of your fist, and it never stops.
Used blood, low on oxygen, comes back from the body into its right side.
The right side pumps it to the lungs, where it picks up fresh oxygen.
Fresh blood comes back from the lungs into the left side.
And the strong left side pumps it out to the whole body. Two pumps beating together, about seventy times a minute.
People have always wanted to write things down.
Long ago, they scratched marks into the sand with a stick.
Then they pressed a cut reed into soft clay.
Later, a bird's feather, a quill, was dipped in ink.
Pencils packed graphite into wood, so you could rub mistakes away.
Fountain pens carried their own ink inside.
And today, a stylus writes with light on a screen.
Different tools, same idea: putting our thoughts where others can read them.
